html:
The potato, first grown in the Andes of South America, reached Spain around 1570 and over the next two centuries became a staple food across much of Europe. The Inca and their neighbours had farmed it for thousands of years and stored it freeze dried.

Europeans were slow to trust it. It was a strange tuber, not a grain, and it was not mentioned in the Bible. For a long time it was grown in gardens or fed to animals. Rulers pushed it: Frederick the Great ordered Prussian peasants to plant it in the 1700s, and Antoine Parmentier promoted it in France.

Once accepted, it changed diets. A field of potatoes fed more people than a field of grain, and it grew in cold, wet places where wheat did poorly. It helped Europe's population grow fast in the 1700s and 1800s.

The danger was dependence on one crop. In Ireland it fed most of the poor, and when blight struck, the result was the Great Famine. See also potato reaches Europe and the wider Columbian Exchange.
